claims.text: Algorithmic fairness can be reformulated as a constrained optimization problem where the objective is to maximize public safety while satisfying formal fairness constraints.
For several past definitions of fairness, optimal constrained algorithms require detaining defendants above race-specific risk thresholds.
The optimal unconstrained decision algorithm requires applying a single, uniform risk threshold to all defendants regardless of race.
There is an inherent tension between improving public safety and satisfying prevailing notions of algorithmic fairness.
In empirical evaluation on Broward County, Florida pretrial data, the trade-off between public safety and algorithmic fairness constraints is large in practice.

evidence.description: Here we reformulate algorithmic fairness as constrained optimization: the objective is to maximize public safety while satisfying formal fairness constraints designed to reduce racial disparities.
We show that for several past definitions of fairness, the optimal algorithms that result require detaining defendants above race-specific risk thresholds.
We further show that the optimal unconstrained algorithm requires applying a single, uniform threshold to all defendants.
Because the optimal constrained and unconstrained algorithms generally differ, there is tension between improving public safety and satisfying prevailing notions of algorithmic fairness.
By examining data from Broward County, Florida, we show that this trade-off can be large in practice.

methodologies.name: Constrained Optimization Framework for Fairness
methodologies.description: Formulates algorithmic decision-making as public safety maximization subject to algorithmic fairness constraints, comparing constrained and unconstrained decision thresholds.
conditions: Comparison of race-specific vs uniform thresholds

limitations.text: Black defendants are substantially more likely than white defendants to be incorrectly classified as high risk in existing decision algorithms.
The empirical demonstration is focused on pretrial release decisions within a single jurisdiction dataset (Broward County, Florida).
